items.body:
Jensen Huang attends a media roundtable meeting in Singapore in December 2023. Photograph: Edgar Su/Reuters

Jensen Huang attends a media roundtable meeting in Singapore in December 2023. Photograph: Edgar Su/Reuters

Jensen Huang’s reported affair was ‘most expensive sex since Helen of Troy’, US senator says

John Kennedy looks to Trump leaders as he asks how China evidently bypassed export controls for Nvidia’s top AI chips

Invoking Greek mythology, US senator John Kennedy has characterized former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy”.

The Louisiana Republican’s allusion to the legendary figure whose desirability was such that it caused the mythic Trojan war came during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday. Host Kristen Welker asked Kennedy, known for his colloquialisms, if US national security was put at risk by Huang’s affair, given the position his company’s chips have occupied at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom.

Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO on 12 November after allegations surfaced of extramarital relationships with the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees.

Howard Lutnick has been Trump’s ally for decades. His ties to Nvidia may spell his downfall

Read more

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been executive director of Megaspeed International. Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, in violation of export controls in the US, where the Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced AI chips to China.

On Sunday’s edition of CNN’s State of the Union, the Trump administration’s national intelligence director, Jay Clayton, said he suspected China was able to obtain Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips.

Kennedy said he was “less interested in … what [Huang] did” than in asking the Trump administration’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, and its treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, about how China was evidently able to circumvent US “export controls”.

“Mr Huang … did what he did. I hope he had a good time. It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy,” Kennedy said.

Lutnick has faced scrutiny over allegedly ignoring warnings that Megaspeed was smuggling chips to China. Other administration leaders, including Bessent, wanted to put Megaspeed on a trade blacklist – but the commerce department stalled enforcement of it.

Kennedy said he could only conclude commerce department leaders are either “so incompetent you wouldn’t put them in charge of a food truck” – or “they knowingly allowed this to happen”.

He said he wanted to get Bessent and Lutnick under oath in front of a Senate committee to “answer some hard questions”.

John Kennedy speaks to the media on 10 November, the day of the Senate Republican caucus leadership elections at the US Capitol in Washington DC. Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters

“And if secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion,” Kennedy said.

Bessent said on Sunday’s edition of CBS News’s Face the Nation that the Trump administration had been in touch with Nvidia’s temporary management, lead directors and lawyers while trying to find out who was in charge of compliance at the company.

“It behooves Nvidia to move ⁠quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was,” Bessent said on the program.

A former Louisiana state treasurer who began his political career as a Democrat before switching parties and becoming a staunch Trump administration ally, Kennedy delivers many of the colloquialisms that have become his calling card with a southern US drawl.

Many believe Kennedy resorts to the drawl to come off as folksy – while he holds degrees from Vanderbilt University, the University of Virginia School of Law and the UK’s Oxford University, and is estimated to be one of the wealthiest US senators.

items.title: US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order
items.summary: The Army says "swift action" is necessary to protect its personnel and nearby communities around its ammunition plant in Iowa.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

ByRebecka Pieder

Updated 39 minutes ago

The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filing shows.

"To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."

The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.

The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The army now plans to act by 24 November under an emergency exemption.

In the new filing, the Department of the Army argued that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion, a risk it said would become more likely as temperatures were set to fall in the coming days.

"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states.

It argued that the army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored in preparation for the detonation and that made the explosives more "vulnerable to temperature changes".

The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.

Earlier, the army had warned residents to leave their homes for six hours on the original scheduled day of the explosion, for the duration of the explosion and until the dust settled. An advisory warned "all humans" to avoid being outside in the affected areas while the demolition detonation was set to take place.

Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the IAAAP found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.

On Friday, the military said it was working with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the explosion was done in the safest manner possible.

Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place was the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.

The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".

One of the Environmental groups suing to pause the detonation, the Iowa Environmental Council, argued that many Iowans living within the risk-zone were unaware that the explosion was scheduled to happen.

"There is no safe level of lead exposure, and Iowans were given just days to prepare for the November 20 detonation," the organisation said in a press statement.

The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, which filed the lawsuit on Thursday that prompted the court-ordered pause, filed a new motion on Sunday in response to the army's filing.

The group asks the court to pause proceedings so that it may submit additional information before the scheduled detonation.

The motion includes declarations from environmental experts and local officials who support pausing the detonation, citing a lack of public notice and questioning the Army's claim that delay would cause significant risks.

items.title: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
items.summary: Finnish defence forces say that Ukraine was likely behind the drone strike on Saturday. Kyiv has yet to comment.
items.body:
Image source, Finnish Border Guard

Image caption,

The Finnish Border Guard is leading the operations involving the Sparta II

ByHafsa Khalil

Updated 43 minutes ago

A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.

The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.

"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."

Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.

The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.

The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.

This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.

Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."

The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.

It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.

Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.

Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.

Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.

The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.

Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

items.summary: EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ and did not mention fossil fuels The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dra…
items.body:
The Cop31 president, Murat Kurum, at the closing plenary session. Photograph: Abdullah Guclu/Anadolu/Getty Images

The Cop31 president, Murat Kurum, at the closing plenary session. Photograph: Abdullah Guclu/Anadolu/Getty Images

Cop31 climate talks break down as key deal rejected

EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ after two weeks of fierce negotiations

Cop31 live blog: longest climate summit ever faces collapse

The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey.

The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”

As the talks, scheduled to end on Friday, dragged on into Sunday afternoon it was clear that the “Antalya pact”, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the summit, would not achieve the consensus needed to pass.

The Antalya pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls for rich countries to provide finance to the poor to help them adapt to the impacts of the climate crisis, and calls on countries to minimise the “overshoot” of the 1.5C global heating threshold, of the Paris agreement.

But it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” that more than 130 countries demanded, and included controversial provisions on “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology that campaigners have said perpetuates fossil fuels.

The presidencies avoided outright collapse of the “conference of the parties” by passing decisions on various related matters, including the “just transition” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to a low-carbon economy.

But Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged there was no agreement on the draft “cover decision” text and so it had not been adopted.

“We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum ⁠such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” he said. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise ⁠that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.”

Many countries, including the EU, UK and many developing countries including small island states and some of the poorest countries, said they could not support the Antalya pact deal, which was supposed to be the “cover decision”, or main outcome, of the Cop.

In a dramatic intervention, O’Brien said on behalf of the EU that it could not accept the final text in its current form. “It fails to meet the moment … We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” He said the EU would not accept a decision “that greenwashes fossil fuels”.

Darragh O’Brien (centre) and Wopke Hoekstra, the EU climate commissioner, speak outside a plenary session at Cop31 on Sunday. Photograph: Khalil Hamra/AP

His intervention was met by applause from the hall, and was later followed by similar objections from Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway.

“This feels like a real line in the sand moment. Countries are standing up to fossil fuel interests and saying no,” said Bill Hare, the chief executive of the advisory group Climate Analytics.

Saudi Arabia defended the decision to include CCS in the text. Other countries, including the Africa group, China and Pakistan, also did not object to the deal, despite some having reservations.

Close to 200 countries have been meeting in Antalya for a fortnight under the joint presidencies of Turkey and Australia, with the overrunning talks marked by long periods of deadlock as countries failed to find common ground.

For many participants, these talks exposed a failure of collective will, particularly of the rich world, to confront the urgency of the climate crisis. Civil society groups, who have a mandated role at the talks, declared it the “worst Cop ever”, while African ministers made a dramatic intervention on Friday saying: “We did not come here to beg.”

Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, summed up the view of many on Friday when he said: “The Cop presidents want to tell us this has been a great Cop. Well, I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst Cop ever.”

On Sunday, he added: “The EU has rejected this text, but it cannot wash its hands of the wreckage it helped create.... For countries facing failed harvests, destroyed homes and mounting debt, this amounts to abandonment by the wealthy nations most responsible for the crisis.

“Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves.”

While extreme weather around the world has worsened this year, claiming tens of thousands of lives in heatwaves, in disasters such as the glacier collapse in Nepal, and in droughts and floods worsened by the supercharged El Niño, the slow speed of the climate negotiations appalled even veteran participants.

“There isn’t the sense of urgency to address these issues. That to me is very frustrating,” said Mary Robinson, a former president of Ireland and former UN climate envoy, as the talks neared their scheduled close. “We have co-presidents who haven’t really been stepping up and giving that leadership.”

items.summary: Dozens of militant Israeli settlers raided communities on Saturday night, setting fire to vehicles and several homes Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposi…
items.body:
Israeli settlers torched cars belonging to Palestinians in the West Bank village of Kafr Malik on Saturday night. Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPA

Israeli settlers torched cars belonging to Palestinians in the West Bank village of Kafr Malik on Saturday night. Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPA

Netanyahu rival condemns settler arson attacks on Palestinian villages in West Bank

Dozens of militant Israeli settlers raided communities on Saturday night, setting fire to vehicles and several homes

Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader, who described them as “Jewish terrorism”.

Dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday, setting fire to about a dozen vehicles and several homes and scrawling racist graffiti. At least four communities were attacked. Israeli police said they had launched an investigation with forensic teams.

Photographs from Kafr Malik, near Ramallah, showed one slogan written in Hebrew that read: “This is the first revenge.” Several vehicles and homes had been set alight in the village.

Images from nearby Deir al-Sudan showed vehicles on fire. Palestinian reports said an agricultural building had been set ablaze in Deir Ballut and cars torched in Deir Abu Mashal.

A Palestinian man inspects the damage after the attack. Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPA

An ⁠inconclusive election last month stripped Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, of his majority. Eisenkot has been asked to form a government, though his prospects seem little better.

Referring to the far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, he added: “The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy.”

items.title: Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
items.summary: At least three people were killed and many more feared dead after a fire at a confectionary factory.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

At least three people have been killed and 36 were still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory in western Java on Saturday.

Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for the missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.

Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.

The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.

Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire.

Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.

"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.

Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP.

Firefighters had been called to the building at 1630 local time (0930 GMT) but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz.

"When we arrived (on location)... a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company's protection system was functioning properly or not," he said.

The factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, according to search and rescue authorities.

On LinkedIn the company describes itself as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.

items.summary: UN patron Lewis Pugh saw ships ablaze and fighter jets overhead during three-day swim as Iran conflict continues A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the strait of Hormuz to highlight the environmental cost of the Iran war. Lewis Pugh, a UN patron of the oceans, swam th…
items.body:
Lewis Pugh during his three-day, 9.3-mile swim through the strait of Hormuz. Photograph: Lewis Pugh Foundation/AP

Lewis Pugh during his three-day, 9.3-mile swim through the strait of Hormuz. Photograph: Lewis Pugh Foundation/AP

Briton swims length of strait of Hormuz to highlight environmental cost of war

UN patron Lewis Pugh saw ships ablaze and fighter jets overhead during three-day swim as Iran conflict continues

A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the strait of Hormuz to highlight the environmental cost of the Iran war.

Lewis Pugh, a UN patron of the oceans, swam the 9.3-mile (15km) length of the waterway, which is a key route for oil shipments from the Middle East.

According to the Lewis Pugh Foundation, he witnessed several attacks on commercial shipping, explosions in the distance and fighter jets overhead.

An oil tanker was struck by a projectile about 2.5 miles from where he was swimming on the first day. On the second, he saw flames rising above a headland separating him from a burning liquefied petroleum gas carrier, Tara Gas, and later he passed close to the vessel while it was still on fire.

“My immediate thoughts were for the seafarers onboard,” Pugh said. “The flames were enormous. These vessels carry highly flammable gases, and an attack on one can have catastrophic consequences, not just for crew members but also on the surrounding marine environment.”

A vessel on fire in the strait of Hormuz. Photograph: Lewis Pugh Foundation/AFP/Getty Images

The 56-year-old undertook his first swim in a conflict zone to urge an end to the fighting, the reopening of the strait and action to address environmental damage caused by the conflict.

Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems

Read more

Believed to be the first person to attempt a long-distance swim in the strait since the conflict began in March, Pugh swam a route from Musandam Island, carving through the dramatic mountains and inlets of Oman’s Musandam peninsula and Iran’s spectacular mangrove forests, to reach the Cape of Hormuz at the peninsula’s northern tip.

He said: “War causes immense human suffering. Lives are lost, families are torn apart and homes, hospitals and schools can be destroyed in minutes. But there is another casualty that receives far too little attention: nature itself. And the damage can last long after the fighting has stopped.”

The small expedition team included a support boat and kayak that remained alongside Pugh during the swim.

Pugh said environmental damage caused by conflict often received less attention than the human cost. According to the UN, at least 175 vessels have been attacked since fighting began, and about 30 attacks have caused significant pollution.

Pugh, 56, is a UN patron of the oceans. Photograph: Lewis Pugh Foundation/AFP/Getty Images

The strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most important shipping routes and is also home to wildlife including dugongs, sea turtles and whale sharks.

Pugh, who was born in Plymouth, said oil spills and other contamination could have long-term consequences for marine ecosystems including coral reefs, seagrass meadows and mangrove forests.

items.summary: Choi Kyo-jin says he ‘failed to prepare adequately’ for entrance exams following last-minute scramble to tighten measures South Korea’s education minister has resigned after an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted in the lead-up to key university entrance exams last week. The country has been g…
items.body:
Students at a high school in Seoul during South Korea's annual suneung exams, which this year were upended by an AI cheating scandal. Photograph: Jintak Han/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

Students at a high school in Seoul during South Korea's annual suneung exams, which this year were upended by an AI cheating scandal. Photograph: Jintak Han/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

South Korea education minister resigns after AI cheating scandal engulfs university exams

Choi Kyo-jin said he ‘failed to prepare adequately’ for entrance exams, which this year had phones banned and checks for cameras hidden in clothing

South Korea’s education minister resigned on Sunday after an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted in the lead-up to the country’s key university entrance exams.

The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday, when the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial university entrance exam known as the suneung.

The confession sent officials scrambling to roll out a slew of preventive measures for the entrance exams last week, including blocking public wifi in testing areas.

But the education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, struggled to reassure the public, and teachers’ unions criticised the government response as belated.

South Korea’s high-stakes university exams upended by AI cheating scandal

Read more

The annual eight-hour suneung determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.

“The exam concluded without any major incidents … However, as the minister in charge, I do not believe I am immune from public criticism that we failed to prepare adequately in advance,” Choi wrote on X.

“Now that the exam is over, I take full responsibility and hereby offer my resignation,” he added.

President Lee Jae Myung accepted his resignation, the presidential office said.

A student turns in her tablet and smartphone at a high school in Seoul ahead of the suneung exams. Photograph: Jintak Han/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

Asked during a parliamentary hearing on Monday whether he was confident that authorities could catch would-be cheaters on exam day, the 72-year-old Choi replied: “Due to my age, I am not confident I could.” His response quickly drew public backlash.

Choi did not appear at press conferences in the days leading up to Thursday’s exam, where a vice minister instead announced the preventive measures.

South Korea goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended. The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre.

In the aftermath of the cheating scandal earlier this month, the government announced that smart devices would have to be turned off and handed in for the suneung, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.

The government also sent emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sounded at full volume and could not be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.

Officials said 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices were identified during Thursday’s exam, nearly half of which were detected through the emergency alerts.

With Agence France-Presse

items.title: UK-EU food deal hailed by British firms: ‘We’re pretty aligned anyway’
items.summary: Exporters welcome end in sight for Brexit checks – but are frustrated that implementation will take so long British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to remove the vast majority of physical checks on food, plants and animal products. The sanitary and phytosanitary (…
items.body:
Iain Barbour (left) and his brother Stuart from Jamieson Brothers, a Scottish seed potato supplier. Photograph: Jamieson Brothers

Iain Barbour (left) and his brother Stuart from Jamieson Brothers, a Scottish seed potato supplier. Photograph: Jamieson Brothers

UK-EU food deal hailed by British firms: ‘We’re pretty aligned anyway’

Exporters welcome end in sight for Brexit checks – but are frustrated that implementation will take so long

British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to remove the vast majority of physical checks on food, plants and animal products.

The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal is expected to benefit Britain’s food exporters and will enable UK delicatessens and other small retailers to import European cheese and wine again, something that became economically unviable because of costly Brexit checks.

The agreement is due to take effect on 1 March 2028 and is also intended to reopen the EU market for UK products including fresh sausages, burgers, seed potatoes and molluscs.

However, several years after the UK left the bloc, upending many decades-old trading arrangements, some food exporters said they would remain cautious until the deal came into force.

“Nobody’s going to believe this until it has actually physically happened,” said Iain Barbour, the operations director of the Scottish seed potato producer Jamieson Brothers.

Seed potatoes were not included in the post-Brexit trade deal after the two sides disagreed over certification, halting exports from the UK to the EU despite Scottish seed potatoes’ high health status classification.

The exclusion particularly hit the Scottish industry, whose farmers were among the biggest exporters for the production of chips and crisps in the world, as well as growers in northern England. Scottish seed potato farmers previously accounted for three-quarters of UK production and the sector was worth about £112m a year.

Ireland and the EU represented a fifth of Jamieson Brothers’ trade before Brexit. The company particularly suffered from the loss of the Irish business, given it grew many varieties that were popular on plates in the north and south of Ireland.

Scottish potato farmers were among the biggest exporters for the production of chips and crisps in the world before Brexit. Photograph: Skully/Alamy

While the company adapted its business to start packing work that would have previously been carried out in the EU, Barbour estimates this change cost about £500,000.

“We evolved, we worked with more partners and that’s what kept the business going,” Barbour said.

Barbour is looking forward to supplying his Irish customers once againHowever, he said it would take at least three years until he could revive varieties that were no longer being grown and were instead stored in a seed bank.

“A lot of Scottish farmers stopped producing varieties that were popular in Ireland as they weren’t desired in England. Varieties that had been going about 100 years were killed off in a couple of years,” he said. “So we’ll have to look at bringing them back.”

The planned implementation of the food deal in March 2028 would also be “a couple of months late for the trade”, given most sales happen at the start of the year and the crops needs to be grown in advance.

Barbour anticipates most growers will be wary and will only fully resume trading in 2029. “People are obviously going to be a little bit hesitant to grow anything until it’s 100% official,” he said.

Devon’s Offshore Shellfish has managed to continue exporting to its European customers despite post-Brexit red tape. Photograph: Offshore Shellfish

British exporters of live bivalve molluscs – the collective term for shellfish including mussels, oysters, clams, cockles and scallops – hope the deal will give the sector a shot in the arm.

The industry is small and specialised. It was valued at less than £12m a year before Brexit, but it is crucial for some coastal communities.

Offshore Shellfish, a family-run business produces rope-grown mussels in the waters of Lyme Bay, Devon, has managed to continue exporting to its European customers despite the administrative burden and occasional blocks by French customs.

skip past newsletter promotion

after newsletter promotion

The company exports the vast majority of the blue mussels it produces. It sends to the Netherlands for processing, before most end up in restaurants or on supermarket shelves in Belgium, where they are prized as a key ingredient in moules-frites, one of the country’s national dishes.

Offshore Shellfish’s Sarah Holmyard says the deal’s provisions are ‘a huge win for us’. Photograph: Offshore Shellfish

Sarah Holmyard, the commercial director of Offshore Shellfish, said the most important detail was an assurance that the deal would allow live bivalve molluscs to be exported even if they did not come from waters with the highest quality rating.

Offshore Shellfish’s farms are in waters which are considered “class A” for most of the year, but before the new SPS deal, any change in water quality to “class B” could have temporarily halted exports.

“That’s a huge win for us because we’ve been pushing and pushing and pushing for that,” Holmyard said.

However, the deal will come too late for those UK shellfish producers that have closed down since Brexit. Three out of four mussel fishing companies in the Menai strait, the channel that separates the north Wales mainland from the island of Anglesey, stopped trading after exports became too difficult.

The promised end of physical border checks on dairy, fish and meat products was welcomed by Rich Clothier, the managing director of Wyke Farms. The Somerset-based cheese and butter maker exports about a quarter of its cheddar to the EU, particularly France, Germany and Spain.

Rich Clothier, the managing director of cheesemaker Wyke Farms, says the deal ‘will save a huge amount of cost and product waste’. Photograph: Josh Campbell

Dairy exports to the EU have been less contentious since Brexit than seed potatoes or mussels, but not without challenges. The removal of veterinary checks is viewed as a significant benefit by Clothier.

“It’s a very bureaucratic process to get everything signed off, in what is not a very modern sort of system,” he said. “The agreement will save a huge amount of cost and product waste as well, because these are perishable.

“Any reduction in friction saves cost, it makes business more efficient. But it is really frustrating that it’s going to take so long [to be implemented] because, to be honest, we’re all pretty aligned anyway.”

UK-EU food deal hailed by British firms: ‘We’re pretty aligned anyway’
Exporters welcome end in sight for Brexit checks – but are frustrated that implementation will take so long
British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to remove the vast majority of physical checks on food, plants and animal products.

The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal is expected to benefit Britain’s food exporters and will enable UK delicatessens and other small retailers to import European cheese and wine again, something that became economically unviable because of costly Brexit checks.
The agreement is due to take effect on 1 March 2028 and is also intended to reopen the EU market for UK products including fresh sausages, burgers, seed potatoes and molluscs.
However, several years after the UK left the bloc, upending many decades-old trading arrangements, some food exporters said they would remain cautious until the deal came into force.
“Nobody’s going to believe this until it has actually physically happened,” said Iain Barbour, the operations director of the Scottish seed potato producer Jamieson Brothers.

Seed potatoes were not included in the post-Brexit trade deal after the two sides disagreed over certification, halting exports from the UK to the EU despite Scottish seed potatoes’ high health status classification.

The exclusion particularly hit the Scottish industry, whose farmers were among the biggest exporters for the production of chips and crisps in the world, as well as growers in northern England. Scottish seed potato farmers previously accounted for three-quarters of UK production and the sector was worth about £112m a year.

Ireland and the EU represented a fifth of Jamieson Brothers’ trade before Brexit. The company particularly suffered from the loss of the Irish business, given it grew many varieties that were popular on plates in the north and south of Ireland.

blocks.alt: A tractor pulls a potato harvester across a Scottish coastal field under cloudy skies

blocks.text: Scottish potato farmers were among the biggest exporters for the production of chips and crisps in the world before Brexit. Photograph: Skully/Alamy
While the company adapted its business to start packing work that would have previously been carried out in the EU, Barbour estimates this change cost about £500,000.
“We evolved, we worked with more partners and that’s what kept the business going,” Barbour said.

Barbour is looking forward to supplying his Irish customers once againHowever, he said it would take at least three years until he could revive varieties that were no longer being grown and were instead stored in a seed bank.

“A lot of Scottish farmers stopped producing varieties that were popular in Ireland as they weren’t desired in England. Varieties that had been going about 100 years were killed off in a couple of years,” he said. “So we’ll have to look at bringing them back.”

The planned implementation of the food deal in March 2028 would also be “a couple of months late for the trade”, given most sales happen at the start of the year and the crops needs to be grown in advance.
Barbour anticipates most growers will be wary and will only fully resume trading in 2029. “People are obviously going to be a little bit hesitant to grow anything until it’s 100% official,” he said.

blocks.alt: A hand holds a cluster of shiny dark mussels from a Lyme Bay shellfish farm

blocks.text: Devon’s Offshore Shellfish has managed to continue exporting to its European customers despite post-Brexit red tape. Photograph: Offshore Shellfish
British exporters of live bivalve molluscs – the collective term for shellfish including mussels, oysters, clams, cockles and scallops – hope the deal will give the sector a shot in the arm.
The industry is small and specialised. It was valued at less than £12m a year before Brexit, but it is crucial for some coastal communities.

Offshore Shellfish, a family-run business produces rope-grown mussels in the waters of Lyme Bay, Devon, has managed to continue exporting to its European customers despite the administrative burden and occasional blocks by French customs.

The company exports the vast majority of the blue mussels it produces. It sends to the Netherlands for processing, before most end up in restaurants or on supermarket shelves in Belgium, where they are prized as a key ingredient in moules-frites, one of the country’s national dishes.

blocks.alt: Sarah Holmyard, of Offshore Shellfish, poses in waterproof overalls and a life jacket by the sea

blocks.text: Offshore Shellfish’s Sarah Holmyard says the deal’s provisions are ‘a huge win for us’. Photograph: Offshore Shellfish

Sarah Holmyard, the commercial director of Offshore Shellfish, said the most important detail was an assurance that the deal would allow live bivalve molluscs to be exported even if they did not come from waters with the highest quality rating.

Offshore Shellfish’s farms are in waters which are considered “class A” for most of the year, but before the new SPS deal, any change in water quality to “class B” could have temporarily halted exports.
“That’s a huge win for us because we’ve been pushing and pushing and pushing for that,” Holmyard said.

However, the deal will come too late for those UK shellfish producers that have closed down since Brexit. Three out of four mussel fishing companies in the Menai strait, the channel that separates the north Wales mainland from the island of Anglesey, stopped trading after exports became too difficult.

The promised end of physical border checks on dairy, fish and meat products was welcomed by Rich Clothier, the managing director of Wyke Farms. The Somerset-based cheese and butter maker exports about a quarter of its cheddar to the EU, particularly France, Germany and Spain.

blocks.alt: Rich Clothier of Wyke Farms smells a cheese sample beside a wooden crate

blocks.text: Rich Clothier, the managing director of cheesemaker Wyke Farms, says the deal ‘will save a huge amount of cost and product waste’. Photograph: Josh Campbell

Dairy exports to the EU have been less contentious since Brexit than seed potatoes or mussels, but not without challenges. The removal of veterinary checks is viewed as a significant benefit by Clothier.

“It’s a very bureaucratic process to get everything signed off, in what is not a very modern sort of system,” he said. “The agreement will save a huge amount of cost and product waste as well, because these are perishable.

“Any reduction in friction saves cost, it makes business more efficient. But it is really frustrating that it’s going to take so long [to be implemented] because, to be honest, we’re all pretty aligned anyway.”

items.title: South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
items.summary: Choi Kyo-jin admits last-minute measures to stop AI-assisted cheating during the college entrance exam caused chaos.
items.body:
Figure caption,

How South Korea tackles cheating on its college entrance exam

ByJaroslav Lukiv

South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.

He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.

A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.

The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.

Image source, EPA/Shutterstock

Image caption,

South Korean high school pupils in Daegu check their answers, a day after the annual college entrance exam

"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.

"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.

The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.

Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.

These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.

His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.

"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.

This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.

This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.

Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.

The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.

It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.

Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.

All this made even honest test takers paranoid.

Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.

Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

items.summary: Members of Congress party clashed with police outside tech company’s offices on Friday The youth wing of India’s main opposition Congress party warned of more protests against Meta’s removal of some of its members’ ⁠accounts, ⁠a day after clashing with ​police outside the tech firm’s locals offices.…
items.body:
Indian Youth Congress members protest outside a Meta office building in Mumbai, India. Photograph: Indian Youth Congress/IYC/Reuters

Indian Youth Congress members protest outside a Meta office building in Mumbai, India. Photograph: Indian Youth Congress/IYC/Reuters

Indian opposition party’s youth wing warns of more Meta protests after police clashes

Members of Congress party clashed with police outside tech company’s offices on Friday

The youth wing of India’s main opposition Congress party warned of more protests against Meta’s removal of some of its members’ ⁠accounts, ⁠a day after clashing with ​police outside the tech firm’s locals offices.

In Hyderabad on Friday, protesters ‌carrying placards and chanted slogans as they stormed into ‌the building that houses Meta’s offices, smashing plants to the ground and clashing with police, according to footage released by the Indian Youth Congress’s X account.

The Indian Youth Congress on Saturday posted warnings on X that it would “storm your offices across the country and stage protests” unless the Instagram accounts of its leaders were restored.

‘Humanity is a privilege’: Umar Khalid on his six years in an Indian jail without trial

Read more

Two such accounts were restored after Friday’s protests, but thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted, Manu Jain, who is in charge of social media for ⁠the youth group, told Reuters on Saturday. Meta must explain how its algorithms restrict posts and must restore accounts taken down ​on government orders, he added.

India is Meta’s biggest market by users and the company declined to comment on Friday’s demonstrations.

Congress members burn signs during a protest in Mumbai. Photograph: Indian Youth Congress/IYC/Reuters

Debate is growing in India about potential ⁠risks to free speech from the increasingly strict efforts of Narendra Modi’s government to remove social media content it objects to. India’s IT ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Meta has said it restricts ​content in India to comply with local laws.

Modi’s government says it orders content to be taken down only if it breaches local laws, can harm public safety ⁠or national security. Congress has long accused Meta and other social media platforms of curbing dissent online by removing accounts.

A video ‌from Friday’s demonstration showed protesters spray-painting anti-Meta slogans on walls outside the building that houses its Mumbai office and clashing with security guards who tried to stop them.

In Gurugram near New Delhi, Congress workers chanted slogans and held banners reading “restore youth Congress accounts”, online posts showed.

An opposition politician from Telangana state criticised Congress workers over what he called vandalism at Meta’s Hyderabad office, saying it ​had undermined the city’s reputation as a safe destination for businesses.

Police clash with Youth Congress members at a protest in Hyderabad. Photograph: Indian Youth Congress/IYC/Reuters

Pradeep Bhandari, a national spokesperson for Modi’s ruling party, also criticised Congress’ actions on Saturday, saying they had “not only vandalised and destroyed Meta’s office in Hyderabad” but were also “flaunting it on social media”.

“This is Congress Model: Vandalise offices of Private companies,” he wrote.

Reporters Without Borders has ​said the removal of journalistic content from social media ​has been on the rise in India this year, and free speech activists say a new government rule gives social media ​companies hardly any time to review ‌and decide on takedown requests.

In ​February, Modi’s government ordered social media companies ​to take down unlawful content within three hours of being notified about it, tightening an earlier 36-hour timeline.

Meta disclosures show that it restricted more than 5.4m posts or accounts in India under local laws in the first half of 2026, second only to Indonesia and up from about 70,000 in the whole of 2025.

“The large majority of these items included instances where we were obligated to proactively restrict content … based on local law requirements,” Meta said.

items.title: Bank of England directors illegally profited from post-abolition enslavement in Cuba
items.summary: New research finds that the British-led Cobre Mining Company helped industrialise Manchester via copper deposits and enslaved African people • Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds British businesses run by long-serving directors of the Bank of England profite…
items.body:
Copper works in the lower Swansea valley, Charles Pascoe Grenfell and El Cobre mine, Cuba. Cobre was ‘likely to be the largest slave enterprise in the western hemisphere’ by the 1840s. Illustration: Guardian Pictures/Alamy

Copper works in the lower Swansea valley, Charles Pascoe Grenfell and El Cobre mine, Cuba. Cobre was ‘likely to be the largest slave enterprise in the western hemisphere’ by the 1840s. Illustration: Guardian Pictures/Alamy

Highly lucrative: Bank of England directors illegally profited from post-abolition enslavement in Cuba

New research finds that the British-led Cobre Mining Company helped industrialise Manchester via copper deposits and enslaved African people

Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds

British businesses run by long-serving directors of the Bank of England profited from “brutal” enslavement in Cuba for decades after slavery’s abolition in the British empire, according to research.

Men and boys were enslaved in prison conditions at the El Cobre copper ore mine near Santiago de Cuba, which supplied British firms during the Industrial Revolution, the historian Chris Evans has found.

In the 1840s, Cuba was the most important foreign source of copper ore for the UK. Copper was critical to Manchester’s cotton industry, railways and telegraphy.

Previous research has revealed that dozens of financiers involved in the founding in 1694 of the Bank of England invested in enslavement.

Now, Evans’s research reveals that ties between key figures in the UK’s financial system and enslavement of African peoples continued even after the government outlawed it.

Britain abolished its trade in enslaved people in 1807 and passed legislation abolishing slavery in most of its empire in 1833.

However, as Britain’s Slavery Abolition Act was coming into force, “City of London figures” were developing mining of El Cobre’s copper ore deposits, an operation which depended on enslavement in Spanish-controlled Cuba.

Key players in the highly lucrative operation included the Bank of England directors Charles Pascoe Grenfell (1790-1867) and William Thompson (1792-1854), acting in a private capacity.

Enslaved copper miners at El Cobre were likely to have been trafficked to Cuba by illegal voyages from the Bight of Biafra, in modern-day Nigeria, as Evans details in his book, Slavery’s Long Goodbye – Capitalism, Nationalism and Christianity in the Age of British Emancipation.

The death rate at El Cobre means it is likely that thousands of Africans were exploited there. Their life stories remain largely undocumented. At the time, slavery was legal in Cuba but the importation of enslaved people was not.

As a partner in the Cobre mining and export company, Grenfell was a driving force in enslaved miners’ exploitation.

Cobre was “likely to be the largest slave enterprise in the western hemisphere” by the 1840s, Evans said. Investors who held Cobre shares from the outset received £102 in dividends for every £40 share between 1836 and 1865.

Enslavement at El Cobre ended after Cuban revolutionaries captured the town from Spanish forces in November 1868. Illustration: Amgueddfa Cymru/National Museum of Wales

Grenfell was also a partner in a Swansea-based smelter Pascoe, Grenfell & Sons, which bought imports from the mine, in an era when the Welsh port was the centre of the global copper trade.

Meanwhile, Thompson, a former lord mayor of London, exploited enslaved miners through the ore export firm he directed, the Royal Santiago Company.

The UK is facing increased pressure to make a formal apology to Caribbean and African nations for Britain’s centuries-long perpetuation of transatlantic chattel slavery. Commonwealth leaders say “structured dialogue” with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, will begin in the next year.

While the Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has claimed Britain has nothing to apologise for, scholarship – dating back to the Trinidadian statesman Eric Williams’s 1944 book, Capitalism and Slavery – reveals the global impact of the colonialism and chattel enslavement that was integral to British capitalism’s success.

Evans, a former professor at the University of South Wales, said: “As Britain ostentatiously winds down its own slave system in the 1830s, British capital is boosting slavery elsewhere in the western hemisphere.

“The illegal trade, involving French and Spanish merchants, was flourishing and substantial. There were British (anti-slavery) patrols off the coast of Cuba, but they’re relatively few in number and intercept only a very small proportion of slave ships.”

Conditions at El Cobre were “extremely brutal”, with daily violence and torture. “Slave catchers” were employed to snatch miners who tried to escape to the mountains.

after newsletter promotion

In 1817, under British pressure, Spanish authorities signed a treaty that banned trafficking enslaved Africans to Cuba. But as Cuba’s sugar and coffee plantations relied on enslaved African workers, local colonial authorities ignored it, with 25,000 captives arriving in 1859 alone.

Charles Grenfell was a partner in a Swansea-based smelter Pascoe, Grenfell & Sons, which bought imports from Cuba. Illustration: Digitised by Bethan Jones/Amgueddfa Cymru/National Museum of Wales

In 1843, pressure from the British and Foreign Anti-Slavery Society prompted legislation intended to prohibit British subjects from owning enslaved people in other jurisdictions, after undercover investigations exposed British mining companies’ activities in Brazil and Cuba, including at El Cobre.

But after lobbying by mining interests, parliament diluted the legislation, allowing companies to retain enslaved workers as their “property” and hire others. The concessions prompted abolitionists to withdraw their support for the law, which failed to end the exploitation.

Neither Grenfell nor Thompson appears to have faced legal penalties for their involvement. Grenfell became the Liberal MP for Preston in the late 1840s, later boasting that his father had been an abolitionist. Grenfell remained a B of E director until 1864.

Enslavement at El Cobre finally ended after Cuban revolutionaries captured the town from Spanish forces in November 1868. The rebel commander proclaimed the miners’ emancipation on New Year’s Eve, and formerly enslaved workers later joined Cuba’s liberation army.

Evans’s book explores Britain’s overlapping histories of slavery, capitalism and missionary Christianity through the lives of Grenfell and two of his cousins.

Evans added: “The British in the early 19th century had started to understand slavery as a national sin.

“In the classical age of abolition, you could do things like abstain from eating sugar from the West Indies.

“But with copper, you can’t do that because it’s embodied in the industrial world, and, in the age of joint-stock capitalism, you have many British people who invest in mining companies who genuinely didn’t know these companies were using enslaved workers.

“Slavery was rendered invisible by the complexity of industrial society. But British engagement with slavery continued long after Emancipation. It involved the mercantile-financial elite of London as well as hundreds, possibly thousands, of rank-and-file investors from the Victorian middle class.”

A Bank of England spokesperson said: “We have previously acknowledged the role of former governors and directors in the slave trade.”

Conditions at El Cobre were “extremely brutal”, with daily violence and torture. “Slave catchers” were employed to snatch miners who tried to escape to the mountains.

In 1817, under British pressure, Spanish authorities signed a treaty that banned trafficking enslaved Africans to Cuba. But as Cuba’s sugar and coffee plantations relied on enslaved African workers, local colonial authorities ignored it, with 25,000 captives arriving in 1859 alone.

In 1843, pressure from the British and Foreign Anti-Slavery Society prompted legislation intended to prohibit British subjects from owning enslaved people in other jurisdictions, after undercover investigations exposed British mining companies’ activities in Brazil and Cuba, including at El Cobre.

But after lobbying by mining interests, parliament diluted the legislation, allowing companies to retain enslaved workers as their “property” and hire others. The concessions prompted abolitionists to withdraw their support for the law, which failed to end the exploitation.

Neither Grenfell nor Thompson appears to have faced legal penalties for their involvement. Grenfell became the Liberal MP for Preston in the late 1840s, later boasting that his father had been an abolitionist. Grenfell remained a B of E director until 1864.

Enslavement at El Cobre finally ended after Cuban revolutionaries captured the town from Spanish forces in November 1868. The rebel commander proclaimed the miners’ emancipation on New Year’s Eve, and formerly enslaved workers later joined Cuba’s liberation army.
Evans’s book explores Britain’s overlapping histories of slavery, capitalism and missionary Christianity through the lives of Grenfell and two of his cousins.
Evans added: “The British in the early 19th century had started to understand slavery as a national sin.
“In the classical age of abolition, you could do things like abstain from eating sugar from the West Indies.

“But with copper, you can’t do that because it’s embodied in the industrial world, and, in the age of joint-stock capitalism, you have many British people who invest in mining companies who genuinely didn’t know these companies were using enslaved workers.

“Slavery was rendered invisible by the complexity of industrial society. But British engagement with slavery continued long after Emancipation. It involved the mercantile-financial elite of London as well as hundreds, possibly thousands, of rank-and-file investors from the Victorian middle class.”
A Bank of England spokesperson said: “We have previously acknowledged the role of former governors and directors in the slave trade.”

items.title: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
items.summary: Fausto Isidro "Chapo Idisro" Meza Flores, who is accused of drug trafficking and torture, is detained after gun fight with authorities.
items.body:
Image source, FBI

Image caption,

Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained by Mexican special forces on Friday

ByTara Mewawalla

A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.

Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained along with his lieutenant by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.

Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.

Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.

Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores and his second-in-command, it added.

Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

A number of vehicles were pictured burning on a highway near Los Mochis, Sinaloa, after Fausto Isidro "Chapo Idisro" Meza Flores was arrested

The two detainees were subsequently flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said.

When he was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.

Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.

He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.

The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.

Meza Flores was originally a high-ranking member of the Beltrán Leyva Organization, but a split between rival factions led to a surge of violence and prompted him to establish his own cartel by 2013.

His organisation has also engaged in what US officials described as an "extremely violent turf war" with the Sinaloa Cartel, one of the most powerful drug trafficking gangs, which operates in the same region.

Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list after Mexican authorities reportedly linked his cartel to 20 million fentanyl pills they seized in 2024.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has taken a tougher stance on the country's cartels in a bid to resist US intervention on Mexican soil. Mexico has welcomed closer collaboration but resisted US boots on the ground.

Trump made stemming the flow of drugs into the US across its southern border one of his key election pledges.

items.title: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
items.summary: The National Crime Information Center database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

ByJaroslav Lukiv

Updated 1 hour ago

The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media reports, citing two people briefed on the issue.

The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks.

It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US. The agency did not immediately respond to the BBC's request for comment.

When asked about the breach in a Fox News interview on Saturday, President Donald Trump said he had "just heard" about the hack. "I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he said.

"But maybe we'll learn things that we would've never learned otherwise," the president added.

This apparent breach of FBI database comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyberattacks, but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.

White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with US President Donald Trump saying he was not good enough.

In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.

After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.

In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) .

Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.

The USDA has not publicly commented on the issue.

items.title: Nigerian youth have shown their power in the past - why aren't they shaping this election?
items.summary: Fewer young people have registered to vote in next year's election than in 2023 - are young people losing faith in democracy?
items.body:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Bola Tinubu (in red hat) would be 79 at the end of a second term, if he is re-elected

ByMansur Abubakar

Reporting fromAbuja

Abdulhadi Dalhatu is something of a rarity in Nigeria politics.

At 38, he is among the young people seeking elected office in a country where about 80% of the population is under 40.

He hopes his age will stand in his favour as he campaigns for a seat in the state assembly in the northern Kano state in January's general elections.

"Younger people are the majority in this country and should be deciding the future," Dalhatu tells the BBC.

But Nigeria's political history suggests he faces an uphill battle.

Since the return to civilian rule in 1999, Goodluck Jonathan has been the youngest person elected president, taking office at the age of 53.

The current president, Bola Tinubu, is 74 and would be 79 by the end of a second term if he is re-elected in January.

His main challengers are also considerably older. Atiku Abubakar, seeking the presidency for the seventh time, is 79, while Peter Obi is 65.

Of the 18 presidential candidates, only one is under 40 - Moses Olusoji Adebisi, a 35-year-old businessman representing the Democratic Leadership Alliance (DLA).

Although he says he is confident of winning, few Nigerians appear to know much about him and he has not been seen much on the campaign trail.

The contrast is striking in a country with one of the world's youngest populations, where young people have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to shape political debate and mobilise for change.

In the previous election, Obi, then 61, galvanised millions of young Nigerians through a social media-driven movement known as the "Obedients".

His campaign promised a break from the established political order, appealing particularly to young people struggling to find jobs and earn a decent living.

But his failure to win the presidency left many of his supporters disillusioned.

"At the time we were so hopeful, but unfortunately the result wasn't what we wanted, which made many lose hope in the system," former Obedient Nonso Chukwudi tells the BBC.

The movement had built on the momentum of the EndSars protests in 2020, which grew into one of Nigeria's biggest youth-led movement in decades.

Initially sparked by anger over police brutality, the demonstrators developed into a wider call for political reform, accountability and greater youth participation in governance.

But the protests were eventually crushed by the authorities. About 56 were reportedly killed, although officials dispute this figure, while hundreds were arrested and some had their bank accounts frozen.

Both EndSars and the Obedients demonstrated the capacity of young Nigerians to mobile around political causes.

Image source, Abdulhadi Dalhatu

Image caption,

Abdulhadi Dalhatu hopes to be president one day but bemoans the financial obstacles needed to contest

But turning that enthusiasm into sustained electoral participation has proved much harder.

Hajara Musa, 33, is among those who have lost faith in the political system. She has no plans to register or vote in the near future.

"I just feel like things are already determined and I'll just be wasting my time. It is going to be the same people all over again," she tells the BBC.

The electoral register appears to reflect this growing disillusionment.

Although the number of registered voters has increased by 10 million to over 103 million since the last election, enrolment of those under 35 has actually fallen, by about seven million.

Young people now account for just 29% of registered voters, down from 40% in 2023.

Nigeria's electoral commission, Inec, says it has made efforts to encourage more young people to register ahead of the 2027 general elections.

This includes appointing nine ambassadors from the entertainment industry, spanning film, music and comedy, to reach younger audiences.

But the figures suggest these efforts have yet to make a significant difference.

Dalhatu says he understands the frustration but argues that young Nigerians cannot expect change, if they stay away from the political process.

"Unfortunately, many prefer to just post on social media" instead of getting involved, he says.

Of course being young does not mean you are necessarily the best candidate.

For those who want to participate, there is a formidable obstacle to getting into politics - money.

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Young people now account for just 29% of registered voters, down from 40% in 2023

Dalhatu dreams of becoming president one day, but says he has previously had to abandon campaigns because he could not raise enough funds.

The cost of running for office in Nigeria is notoriously high.

Under the Electoral Act, presidential candidates were allowed to spend up to 5bn naira (£2.8m; $3.7m) on campaigns ahead of the 2023 elections. That spending limit has since been doubled.

The cost of nomination forms alone puts the presidency beyond the reach of most aspiring young Nigerians.

The ruling All Progressive Congress (APC), along with the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and the African Democratic Congress (ADC) have each set their presidential nomination fee at 100m naira ($74,000; £56,000), making it extremely hard for new challengers to emerge.

Since the return to democracy in 1999, only two parties have governed Nigeria - the PDP from 1999 to 2015 and the APC since 2015.

These parties, alongside the ADC, formed last year by politicians who had defected from the other two, have established nationwide network of branches, supporters and campaigners.

Those aspiring candidates without the financial resources to secure nomination forms and compete in the internal party contests of the main parties have little chances of becoming president.

The barriers are also evident in the National Assembly.

Not one of Nigeria's 109 senators is under 40, while only 14 of the 360 members of the House of Representatives fall into that age group.

"I have been in politics for many years and I will tell you that young people in this country lack the resources to become president," says Dalhatu, who is running under Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Atiku Abubakar is seeking the presidency for a seventh time

Fatima Zahra Umar, a young politician in the APC who has previously tried to run for a seat in the House of Representatives, agrees.

"Young Nigerians are poor. Nigerian politics is cash-intensive, so participation is guided by money," she says, adding that young people are often content with having a bit of influence as a special advisor to a senior politician.

But political analyst Seun Ajayi believes the problems go beyond the financial barriers.

"We have some of the most brilliant young persons in the world, but they are either not interested in politics or feel satisfied when given a small role in government," he says.

"The old men are not going to sit idle and allow us to push them out. We have to fight for the big positions, but at the moment I don't see the zeal."

Umar believes changing attitudes towards young leadership is equally important.

"Culturally, we are not primed to trust or accept the brilliance of a younger person, so it will be very difficult," she says.

"Old men are still holding on to the system."

Some Nigerians took inspiration from the wave of success of young candidates in the recent midterm elections in the US, some of whom have roots in Africa.

"America Has Done It, Can Nigerians Do the Same?" entertainer Charly Boy wrote on X, in a post that was widely shared.

He said the US results served as a warning to Nigerian politicians that no matter how powerful the political machine, voters can change the direction of government.

He called on young people to interrogate candidates about their past promises: "Has life improved? Where are the jobs, security and affordable living?

"Democracy is not a spectator sport, nor is it about sharing rice," he wrote.

items.title: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl
items.summary: When 16-year-old Landon Tresp met a teenage girl in an online game, it led to him and his mother helping the FBI rescue her from kidnapping.
items.body:
Image source, Submitted photo

Image caption,

Landon Tresp, 16, left, met the girl playing Among Us before alerting his mother, Khristina, 41, to the missing teen's predicament

BySheila Flynn

Senior US Reporter, Reporting fromColorado

Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when he began chatting on his laptop with another player.

She was also a teenager, and the pair "kind of just clicked," he tells the BBC.

He told her he liked her name, and she confessed that it was an alias. She was a runaway, she said - and was being held against her will, hundreds of miles from home, though she didn't know exactly where. The girl, 17, and had been missing for more than a year.

Stunned, Landon felt "helpless," he says - and, after learning more details over two weeks of chatting, he decided to tell his mother, Khristina on 31 October this year. The 41-year-old nurse and mother of five was putting Halloween makeup on her younger children for trick-or-treating when he briefed her.

That set the mother and son on a path to track down his friend, contact her mother, cooperate with the FBI - and ultimately witness the rescue of the teen - only 24 hours after Landon first alerted Khristina to her plight.

"She had one opportunity to reach out her hand and ask for help, and she chose me," Khristina says of the girl, who was 15 when she went missing.

Image source, Khristina Tresp

Image caption,

A screenshot shows Khristina on a call with the girl as she showed her the knife her alleged captor kept under his pillow

The Tresps have shared with BBC screenshots of communication with the girl and a photo matching the criminal complaint to corroborate their story.

Landon first told his mother about "Jenny" - whose identity the BBC is protecting - in mid-October, a few weeks before the rescue.

"He had mentioned something about maybe a week or so into talking to her that he met a girl online, and she was really sweet," says Khristina - who cautioned him that "you don't always know who's on the other side of the screen".
